# Inverse concave arms and exact centered-cap linearization

This is the horizontal-tangent case b0=0 of the profile problem in `candidate 5b3b585d1663ccd0`. It proves the deletion representation and general-dimensional formulas. The localization observation at the end is conditional; no existence, multiplier, or finite-knot theorem is asserted.

## 1. The two inverse arms

Let d=m+1>=2 and let r be a positive concave profile on [a,b], where a<0<b. Assume its maximum r0 is attained at zero. For 0<=v<=r0 define

    A_+(v)=max{z>=0:r(z)>=v},
    A_-(v)=max{-z:z<=0, r(z)>=v}.

Both functions are nonnegative, nonincreasing, and concave. Indeed a convex combination of two points on one side with heights at least v1,v2 has height at least the same convex combination of v1,v2; taking endpoint limits gives the concavity inequality for the inverse arm. The functions are continuous on the interior and have the natural endpoint values obtained from the closed superlevel sets.

A positive A_+(r0) or A_-(r0) records a flat top of the profile. Constant initial pieces of the arms record positive endpoint heights of the original truncated profile. Neither phenomenon is discarded. At every v<r0 both arms are positive because the source is interior and r is continuous.

The common planar measure is f(x,z)=r(z)^(m-1)/2 on |x|<=r(z). Its mass is

    V=m int_0^r0 v^(m-1)[A_+(v)+A_-(v)]dv.          (1)

This follows from the nonnegative layer identity r(z)^m=int_0^r(z) m v^(m-1)dv and Tonelli.

## 2. Exact deletion records, including truncation

For s>0 let

    eta_s(dq)=(1/2)r(sq)^(m-1)
       1_{sq in[a,b]} 1_{|q|<=r(sq)}dq.

Here the density is zero outside the original interval, and no undefined zero power is used when m=1. Along every fixed nonzero q this density decreases with s. Let rho(dq,dt) be its deletion measure, so eta_s is its surviving q marginal at times t>s, up to choices on null boundary sets.

For q of sign epsilon and a_q=|q| in(0,r0), its deletion-time measure is the pushforward under

    t=A_epsilon(v)/a_q

of the following measure in v:

    (1/2)[a_q^(m-1) delta_(a_q)
           +(m-1)v^(m-2)1_(a_q,r0)(v)dv].          (2)

When m=1 only the first term is present. Formula (2) follows from the exact layer identity

    r^(m-1)1_{r>=a_q}
      =a_q^(m-1)1_{r>=a_q}
          +int_(a_q)^r0 (m-1)v^(m-2)1_{r>=v}dv.

The level v survives along the q ray precisely until s=A_epsilon(v)/a_q. A constant arm interval may push an interval of v values to one deletion time; these atoms are included by (2). The set q=0 has zero dq measure and contributes no missing mass at infinite time.

Integrating the bracket in (2) gives r0^(m-1)/2. Thus rho has the SAME uniform q marginal

    rho(dq x [0,infinity))=(r0^(m-1)/2)1_[-r0,r0](q)dq. (3)

The raw component data satisfy

    C(s)=rho{t>s},
    M(s)=s int_(t>s) q d rho,
    P(s)-V/2=int (t-s)_+ q d rho,
    V=2 int t|q| d rho.                              (4)

The first two equalities are the section formulas. For the third, integrate P'(s)=-M(s)/s from s to infinity and use P(infinity)=V/2. Absolute integrability follows from the fourth equality. To verify that fourth equality directly, integrate (2) first in a_q: on one arm the result is

    int t|q| d rho
      =(m/2)int_0^r0 v^(m-1)A_epsilon(v)dv,

which is half that arm's volume contribution in (1). All boundary truncations are already included in the inverse arm and its possible constant pieces.

## 3. Closed formulas at a fixed slope

For one inverse arm A and slope s>0 put

    a_s=max{v in[0,r0]:A(v)>=s v}.

The intersection is unique if a_s<r0, with A(a_s)=s a_s. If a_s=r0, the weaker inequality A(r0)>=s r0 is allowed. Since A is nonincreasing and sv is increasing, the surviving comparison is A(v)>=sv exactly for v<=a_s, up to endpoints.

Define the one-arm coarea C_s(A), positive vertical moment K_s(A), and positive cap-bias contribution J_s(A). For m>=2 they have the exact formulas

    C_s(A)=a_s^m/2
       +(m-1)/(2s) int_(a_s)^r0 v^(m-2) A(v)dv,     (5)

    K_s(A)=s a_s^(m+1)/4
       +(m-1)/(4s) int_(a_s)^r0 v^(m-2) A(v)^2dv,   (6)

    J_s(A)=(m/2) int_0^(a_s) v^(m-1)A(v)dv
          -s a_s^(m+1)/4
       +(m-1)/(4s) int_(a_s)^r0 v^(m-2) A(v)^2dv.   (7)

The same formulas hold for m=1 after omitting all terms with coefficient m-1. For the actual two arms,

    C(s)=C_s(A_+)+C_s(A_-),
    M(s)=K_s(A_+)-K_s(A_-),
    P(s)-V/2=J_s(A_+)-J_s(A_-).                    (8)

Proof. In (2), at a fixed level v the surviving q magnitudes satisfy

    0<=a_q<=min(v,A(v)/s).

For v<=a_s this upper endpoint is v; for v>=a_s it is A(v)/s. Here are the separate atomic and continuous contributions; put a=a_s and R=r0. The atom in (2) is at level v=q, so it survives precisely for 0<=q<=a.

    C_atom=(1/2)int_0^a q^(m-1)dq=a^m/(2m),

    C_cont=(m-1)/2 int_0^R v^(m-2)min(v,A(v)/s)dv
          =(m-1)a^m/(2m)
             +(m-1)/(2s)int_a^R v^(m-2)A(v)dv.

Their sum is (5). Likewise

    K_atom=(s/2)int_0^a q^m dq
          =s a^(m+1)/(2(m+1)),

    K_cont=(m-1)s/4 int_0^R v^(m-2)min(v,A(v)/s)^2dv
          =s(m-1)a^(m+1)/(4(m+1))
             +(m-1)/(4s)int_a^R v^(m-2)A(v)^2dv.

Their sum is (6). Finally the cap-bias kernel is (t-s)_+q=(A(v)-sq)_+, so

    J_atom=(1/2)int_0^a q^(m-1)[A(q)-sq]dq,

    J_cont=(m-1)/2 int_0^R v^(m-2)
                         int_0^min(v,A(v)/s)[A(v)-sq]dq dv
          =(m-1)/2 int_0^a v^(m-1)A(v)dv
             -s(m-1)/4 int_0^a v^m dv
             +(m-1)/(4s)int_a^R v^(m-2)A(v)^2dv.

Adding J_atom gives the coefficient m/2 on the first A integral and the term -s a^(m+1)/4, which is (7). When m=1 every continuous contribution is absent, rather than evaluated through a formal v^-1 factor. All these calculations also cover a_s=R without imposing equality at that endpoint. QED.

At s=0 the one-arm formulas are C_0(A)=r0^m/2, K_0(A)=0, and J_0(A)=(m/2)int_0^r0 v^(m-1)A(v)dv. Thus total C(0)=r0^m and M(0)=0. No expression containing 1/s is used there.

## 4. Centering cancels every quadratic term from the cap objective

Subtract (6) from (7):

    J_s(A)-K_s(A)
      =(m/2)int_0^(a_s) v^(m-1)A(v)dv
            -(s/2)a_s^(m+1).                       (9)

Let nu be any finite probability mixture of slopes whose section moment averages to zero. By (8), its positive and negative K averages agree. Consequently its averaged cap bias can be computed by replacing J by J-K on both arms. Formula (9) shows that, once the intersections a_s are fixed, this averaged cap objective is LINEAR in A_+,A_-. The averaged coarea is likewise linear by (5), and total volume is linear by (1).

For m=1 the moment constraints themselves depend only on the fixed intersections, since K_s(A)=s a_s^2/4. Therefore fixed intersections leave a genuine linear optimization problem over the two concave arms, with their contact equalities or top-saturation inequalities retained.

For m>=2 only the separate centering constraints retain quadratic arm terms. At finitely many fixed slopes, on each interval between their intersection values, their Lagrangian together with any fixed linear cap, volume, and coarea objective has the form

    int v^(m-2)[(A1 v+A0) A(v)+A2 A(v)^2]dv,       (10)

with constants A1,A0,A2 on that interval, separately for each arm. The dimension enters through the common positive weight v^(m-2), not through competing powers of A.

Thus, IF a valid multiplier argument is available and IF unrestricted two-sided local variations of an arm are admissible on an interval, its Euler equation is

    A1 v+A0+2A2 A(v)=0.

When A2!=0 this forces the arm to be affine there. When A2=0, it either gives no stationary arm or is identically zero. This observation does not treat singular curvature, active concavity constraints, existence of extrema, abnormal multipliers, or zero-load intervals. It is an exact algebraic simplification toward a localization argument, not a proved localization theorem or a bound on the number of knots.

All mixtures in Section4 are centered separately within one orientation. No signed cancellation between different cap orientations is substituted for that condition.
